clue.text: Closing plant? Case of farewell, have fun in retirement

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside, so the first and last letters of farewell are taken
retiring means drawing back, so the word for having fun is read backwards

parts.note: to have fun is to party

explanation.surface: A send-off for a retiree: say goodbye and enjoy the party now work is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case of' takes the outer letters of 'farewell'; 'in retirement' reverses the party word, retiring meaning drawing back.
explanation.definitionFit: A Venus flytrap is a carnivorous species whose leaves snap shut on insects, hence a plant that closes.

clue.text: Upset friend has left: brilliant mathematician

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the word for friend is read backwards

parts.note: a pal is a friend
ace means excellent or brilliant

explanation.surface: An upset friend has walked out on a brilliant mathematician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reverses PAL to LAP; Pierre-Simon Laplace was the French mathematician.
explanation.definitionFit: Laplace was an 18th-century French scholar famous for celestial mechanics and the Laplace transform.

clue.text: Tango close to body

parts.note: Tango is T in the NATO phonetic alphabet
or so means approximately, close to a figure

explanation.surface: Tango dancers hold their partners close to the body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close to' looks like a positional signal but is the phrase 'or so'.
explanation.definitionFit: The torso is the trunk of the human body, without head or limbs.

clue.text: Country song about American hotel, essentially

indicators.note: about means around, so the song wraps the other letters

parts.note: an aria is a song in opera
US is short for United States, hence American

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its central letter

explanation.surface: A country-and-western number about an American hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country' suggests a music genre beside 'song', but it is the definition; 'about' wraps the song round the other letters, and 'essentially' picks the centre of 'hotel'.
explanation.definitionFit: Austria is a nation in central Europe whose capital is Vienna.

clue.text: Wear belt

definitions.meaning: British slang for clothes or gear

explanation.definitionFit: Clobber is informal for one's clothing, and as a verb is slang for striking someone, like a belt or thump.

clue.text: Line to put into program for computer

indicators.note: the word to is inserted in the word for program

parts.note: an app is an application program

explanation.surface: Writing a line of code into a program on the computer.
explanation.definitionFit: A laptop is a portable personal machine light enough to rest on one's knees.

clue.text: Football team with tendency to cross, winning corner at the end

indicators.note: winning means gaining, so the word for tendency takes in a letter

parts.note: a bent is a natural tendency or inclination

indicators.note: the final letter of corner is taken

parts.note: to ford a river is to cross it

explanation.surface: A football side prone to crossing, earning a corner late in the game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'winning' puts R, the end of 'corner', inside BENT; Brentford is a London club.
explanation.definitionFit: Brentford FC is an English professional football club based in west London.

clue.text: Comes out of European Union, mostly with backing of idiots

indicators.note: mostly means most of the word, losing its final letter

parts.note: a merger is a union of firms

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter, here of idiots

explanation.surface: Brexit politics: leaving the EU, supported mostly by fools.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts MERGE from MERGER; 'backing of' gives S, the end of 'idiots'.
explanation.definitionFit: To emerge is to come out into view from somewhere hidden or enclosed.

clue.text: See 25
Bath Oliver's last in box

parts.note: Bath is the English spa town, so it stands for SPA

indicators.note: the final letter of Oliver is wanted, as signalled by the possessive plus last

explanation.surface: A Bath Oliver is a dry biscuit; this one is the last left in the tin.
explanation.walkthrough: A Bath Oliver is a traditional English biscuit, so the clue reads as one item; split it into Bath and Oliver's last.
explanation.definitionFit: To spar is to box in practice, trading punches with a partner without a full fight.

clue.text: Oliver's compositions? Fine examples

definitions.meaning: Oliver! is a stage musical, a show, so its songs are pieces from a show

explanation.walkthrough: Oliver! is the Lionel Bart musical based on Oliver Twist; the question mark flags the punning reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A showpiece is an item displayed as an outstanding specimen of its kind, a model of excellence.

clue.text: Work party

definitions.meaning: One of the main British political parties

explanation.definitionFit: Labour means toil or exertion, and the Labour Party is the main centre-left party in UK politics.

clue.text: Want to arrange meeting time: hour put in

indicators.note: meeting means joining up with, so the two pieces sit side by side
the hour abbreviation is placed inside the word for arrange

parts.note: to arrange things is to sort them
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Organising a get-together, one fixes a time and adds an hour to the diary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Want' reads as a verb but is the noun meaning lack; 'put in' signals the insertion and 'meeting' joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Want as a noun means a lack or deficiency, which is what a shortage is.

clue.text: Painting with concerning mark inside mount

parts.note: re means about or concerning

indicators.note: the word for mark is placed within the abbreviation for mount

parts.note: MT is the abbreviation for mount, as in a mountain name
a brand is a mark burnt or stamped on something

explanation.surface: A picture with a sticky mark on the inside of its mount.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mount' looks like a picture mount but is the abbreviation for a mountain; 'inside' signals the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: A canvas by the Dutch master is called a Rembrandt, the artist's name standing for his work.

clue.text: Punk band raises excitement at the start

indicators.note: the word for excitement is placed at the front

parts.note: a buzz is a thrill of excitement
to cock an ear or a hat is to raise it

explanation.surface: A punk group whipping up excitement from the first chord.
explanation.walkthrough: The Buzzcocks were a Manchester punk group of the late 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: Buzzcocks are a British punk group known for 'Ever Fallen in Love'.

clue.text: Like to stay in bed and take it easy

indicators.note: the word for like stays within the word for bed

parts.note: a cot is a small bed
as means like, in the way of

explanation.surface: An invitation to have a lie-in and relax.
explanation.definitionFit: To coast is to proceed with little effort, like a bike freewheeling downhill.

clue.text: Tip of tape measure going round collar

indicators.note: the word for measure goes round the single letter

parts.note: size is a measure of how big something is

indicators.note: a tip is an end, here the final letter of tape

explanation.surface: A tailor measuring a neck: the end of the tape goes round the collar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip of' takes E from the end of 'tape'; 'going round' wraps SIZE around it.
explanation.definitionFit: To collar someone is to grab or arrest them, the same as seizing them.

clue.text: Cover of Escort: a celebrity back issue

indicators.note: back means the whole string is read in reverse
the cover of a word is its outside pair of letters

parts.note: a big name is a celebrity

explanation.surface: A celebrity scandal about a paid escort makes the cover of a back issue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses ET + A + NAME to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To issue is to come or flow out from a source, which is what emanate means.

clue.text: Carpet to cover floor

parts.note: to dress something is to cover or clothe it
to floor someone is to knock them down

explanation.surface: Instructions for laying carpet over a floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpet' looks like a floor covering, but here it is a verb meaning to scold.
explanation.definitionFit: To carpet someone is British slang for reprimanding them, exactly as a dressing-down does.

clue.text: Boss with certain way of working to absorb pressure

indicators.note: to absorb means taking in, so the letters close round the pressure abbreviation

parts.note: sure means certain
P is the physics symbol for pressure
MO is modus operandi, a way of working

explanation.surface: A confident manager whose style handles pressure well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to absorb' takes P inside SUREMO.
explanation.definitionFit: A supremo is the person in overall charge, a top manager or chief.

clue.text: Range of understanding after insignificant day: time to stop work

indicators.note: after places the range word following the word for insignificant

parts.note: wee means tiny, insignificant
ken is one's range of knowledge, as in beyond my ken

explanation.surface: After a dull day, you finally understand it is time to clock off.
explanation.walkthrough: Wee is Scottish for small; ken is one's understanding.
explanation.definitionFit: The weekend is the Saturday-Sunday break when most people are off duty.

clue.text: Bob's one hard song to perform

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
an air is a tune or song
to do something is to perform it

explanation.surface: Bob has a difficult song to sing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a man's name, but a bob is a short haircut.
explanation.definitionFit: A bob is a short haircut, so it is one kind of styled cut.

clue.text: Figure with cake and tea getting biscuit at the back

parts.note: a cake of soap is a bar
char is British slang for tea

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, here from biscuit

explanation.surface: Afternoon tea: cake, a cuppa, and a biscuit left at the back of the tin.
explanation.walkthrough: A cake of soap is a bar; char is British slang for tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure in a report is a diagram, and a bar chart is a kind of diagram.

clue.text: Secretary regularly takes breaks

parts.note: PA, a personal assistant, is a secretary
someone who regularly takes a thing uses it

explanation.surface: An office worker who is always going on breaks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' looks like an alternate-letter signal, but here 'regularly takes' is simply USES.
explanation.definitionFit: Pauses are brief stops or rests, the same as short breaks in activity.

clue.text: After reshuffle, Nadine Dorries (Con) out, not primarily being dealt with

indicators.note: a cabinet reshuffle rearranges the ministers, so the letters are rearranged
the first letter of out is dropped

explanation.surface: After a cabinet reshuffle, Tory minister Nadine Dorries is out of the government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not primarily' trims 'out' to UT; 'After reshuffle' scrambles NADINEDORRIESCON plus UT. Nadine Dorries is a British Conservative politician.
explanation.definitionFit: A matter under consideration is currently being looked at or handled, not yet settled.

clue.text: More unfinished canapés, crackers and cheese

indicators.note: crackers means crazy, so the letters are scrambled
a word left unfinished loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Party fare: more canapés, some crackers, and a cheese board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfinished' cuts MOR from 'More'; 'crackers' scrambles MOR with CANAPES.
explanation.definitionFit: Mascarpone is a soft, creamy Italian cheese used in tiramisu.

clue.text: Go out with model to get food

parts.note: a fire or light that goes out dies
the Model T was Ford's famous car, so model gives T

explanation.surface: Taking a fashion model out to dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go out with' reads as dating, but it is DIE, with 'with' joining it to T.
explanation.definitionFit: Diet means the food a person or animal habitually eats.

clue.text: Over bowled from complex period of play

indicators.note: taken from means removed out of the word for complex

parts.note: a complex is a psychological obsession
O is the cricket abbreviation for over
B is the cricket abbreviation for bowled

explanation.surface: A cricket match report: an over bowled from a stretch of play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' removes O and B from the front of OBSESSION.
explanation.definitionFit: A session in cricket is one of the stretches of play between intervals, such as before lunch.

clue.text: Friend forced to accept retirement, primarily by firm

indicators.note: the firm's letters come first, placed before the rest

parts.note: CO is short for company, a firm

indicators.note: the word for forced takes in the letter for retirement

parts.note: made someone do something means forced them
R stands for retired, as in cricket scores

explanation.surface: A worker pushed into early retirement by the company.
explanation.walkthrough: R for retired comes from cricket scorecards; 'to accept' signals the insertion and 'primarily by' puts the firm first.
explanation.definitionFit: A comrade is a companion or fellow member, a close mate.
